This is OnCall P G: an evaluation that asks whether frontier models can change a live production database without taking it down.
I'm a customer engineer at a checkout and payments company.
When a platform change goes wrong, I'm the one hearing from merchants: stuck checkouts, abandoned carts.
Database migrations are a classic way it happens.
GoCardless, a payments company, lost its API for about fifteen seconds this way.
A fast ALTER TABLE queued behind a long read, and every request queued behind it.
Today, AI assistants write a lot of these migrations.
So I asked: do frontier models know how to do this safely?
And when they actually do it, does production survive?
First, I built the obvious eval: predict exactly what Postgres, Linux and Kubernetes will do.
Every answer key came from running the real system.
Six frontier models scored between eighty-seven and eighty-nine, out of eighty-nine.
Knowing is saturated. The real question is whether that knowledge survives contact with a live system.
So OnCall P G hands the model an on-call ticket, and a real Postgres seventeen grades the answer.
The orders table has five million rows. An app writes two hundred transactions a second, and an analytics job keeps long reads open.
The model's script runs in its own container, as a non-superuser.
It passes only if the schema ends up right, and fresh app writes still behave,
no app transaction waits longer than five hundred milliseconds, and no app connection errors.
There is no L L M judge, and no hand-written answer key. Postgres decides.
Here is the difference.
The textbook one-line ALTER TABLE is perfectly valid S Q L.
It queues behind the analytics read, and every checkout write queues behind it.
The app stalls: {DEMO_STALL}.
The safe version waits fifty milliseconds at a time, slips in between reads, and the app barely notices.
Can you trust the grader?
Every ticket ships with independent reference solutions that must pass five runs out of five.
And deliberately wrong scripts, including attempts to game it, that must fail, five times out of five.
The database even caught me: two of my own reference answers were wrong, and one of my checks would have failed a valid answer.
And one of my own tickets, a five-million-row backfill, failed its correct answers three times in ten from disk noise, so it no longer counts toward any score.
And when an agentic I D E quietly read the answer key off my disk, a similarity check exposed it.
Every final answer now comes from a source with no file access.

Frontier models know the playbook. But one ticket breaks even them.
Ticket H one: give every order a public I D.
Opus, Sonnet and Haiku each, in at least one run, added a NOT NULL check marked NOT VALID, before backfilling the data.
NOT VALID means existing rows aren't checked. But Postgres still enforces it on every row that gets updated.
So the app's ordinary quantity update hit an old row, and all eight app connections died.
The schema was perfect. Latency was fine. Only the crashed app gave it away.
A passing Opus run made the same early check, but added a trigger that fills the value on update.
That one trigger is the expertise.
Two honest footnotes.
When the ticket framed the job as repairing data first, every frontier model avoided this trap.
And in my pilot, GPT six point one Sol's retry loop sat in the lock queue ninety-five percent of the time, and starved the app.
Changing only its pause fixed it. On the final prompt, Sol chose a safer loop, so I report it as a hazard, not a headline.
So here's the lesson.
Frontier models have memorized the safe-migration playbook.
What they miss is what the playbook doesn't spell out: a constraint that's not valid, yet still fires; a retry loop that's polite to the database, but not to the app.
You only find those by running the plan against a live system.
Everything you've seen reproduces with three commands.
